lines.text: Chapter three. Build it in four steps.
lines.say: Chapter three. Build it in four steps.

lines.text: Step one: start with your real take-home pay, not your salary.

lines.text: If your pay changes month to month, budget from your lowest normal month, and treat extra as a bonus.

lines.text: Step two: list the fixed bills, the ones that are the same every month.

lines.text: Rent, car payment, phone, insurance, minimum debt payments. These come first.

lines.text: Step three: the yearly bills. Turn each one into a small monthly amount.

lines.text: Method one is 50/30/20, from the 2005 book All Your Worth by Elizabeth Warren and Amelia Warren Tyagi.

lines.text: The appeal: a rule simple enough to remember without a spreadsheet.

lines.text: Of take-home pay: 50% on needs, 30% on wants, 20% on savings or paying down debt.

lines.text: It's simple and flexible. The catch: housing alone is a third of the average budget.

lines.text: Method two is the zero-based budget: give every dollar a job until nothing is left over.
lines.say: Method two is the zero-based budget. You give every dollar a job until nothing is left over.

lines.text: Quick summary: 50/30/20 for simplicity, zero-based for control, pay-yourself-first for low effort.

lines.text: Chapter five. Make it stick.
lines.say: Chapter five. Make it stick.

lines.text: Trick one: automate. Set savings and bills to move on payday, so willpower isn't needed.
lines.say: Trick one. Automate. Set savings and bills to move on payday, so willpower isn't needed.

lines.text: Trick three: a small buffer category for things you can't predict.

lines.text: Trick four: adjust every month. A budget that bends doesn't break.

post.yt_desc:
Americans saved just 4.1% of disposable income in August 2026, and only 63% of adults say they'd cover a $400 surprise with cash or its equivalent. We look at where the average household's $78,535 actually goes, why budgets fail, how to build one in four steps with sinking funds, and how 50/30/20, zero-based and pay-yourself-first budgets compare.
